Banff Sunshine Meadows: A True Island in the Sky 

Few places capture the spirit of the Canadian Rockies like Sunshine Meadows in Banff National Park

By
Riley Fonger
-
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:18
Instaread

As Canada’s first and one of the world’s oldest, Banff National Park has long captivated visitors with its turquoise lakes, towering Rocky Mountain peaks, and alpine scenery. 

Nestled in the heart of the park, and just 15 minutes from the town of Banff, is Sunshine Village, one of Canada’s most illustrious mountain resorts. While celebrated for world-class skiing and Canada’s best snow, summer reveals an entirely different side of the mountain. As the snow melts, Sunshine Village transforms into Sunshine Meadows, an alpine destination renowned for hiking, sightseeing, and some of the most unique wildflower displays in the Canadian Rockies.

Banff Sunshine Meadows

Located 90 minutes west of Calgary, Sunshine Meadows draws visitors for its breathtaking scenery, but its ecological significance is equally remarkable. Part of Banff National Park and recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984, the meadows protect a diverse ecosystem.

More than 53 mammal species, 60 bird species, and countless varieties of alpine flora thrive throughout the landscape. Three pristine lakes add to the scenery, showcasing the brilliant blue hues that have made the park’s waters famous worldwide.

What sets Sunshine Meadows apart is its distinction as Canada’s highest alpine meadow. Perched 7,200 feet above sea level, its unique high-elevation environment supports more than 50 species of wildflowers rarely found along the park’s lower valley trails.

“There’s only a small percentage of this subalpine meadow in the national park, and Sunshine Meadows has the largest percentage of it,” said Jennifer Collison, interpretive program leader at Sunshine Village.

Collison has worked at Sunshine Village since 1994. She describes Sunshine Meadows as “one of the hidden gems of Banff National Park,” where visitors can experience everything from the tiniest wildflowers to Columbia ground squirrels moving through the vegetation.

Each July and August, the meadows reach their peak expression as thousands of wildflowers erupt across the Rockies. “Sunshine has such an array of wildflowers that bloom here,” Collison said. “It’s such a large region where you can look out across meadows and meadows of flowers.”

Yellow glacier lilies are the first blooms of the season, appearing beside melting snowbanks before summer gives way to red Indian paintbrush, purple Arctic lupine, blue alpine forget-me-nots and countless others.

While the wildflowers may be the main attraction, they’re only part of the experience. From panoramic viewpoints and scenic hiking trails to mountaintop dining, guided interpretive programs, and overnight stays, there’s no shortage of ways to spend a full day exploring Sunshine Meadows.

Planning your day

The journey to Sunshine Meadows begins with a 22-minute ride aboard Banff’s biggest gondola. The spacious eight-passenger cabins carry visitors high into the Rockies, climbing 7,200 feet to Sunshine Meadows Village.

Before reaching the trails, visitors can explore attractions including the Sunshine Interpretive Centre, Sunshine Mountain Lodge—Banff’s only mountaintop hotel—and the historic Trapper’s Bar & Grill, opened in 1928 by Canadian Pacific Railway.

From the village, an eight-minute chairlift ride and five minute walks take you to the Standish Viewing Deck. Here, sweeping 360-degree views stretch across three alpine lakes, the surrounding Rocky Mountains, the Monarch Ramparts, and Mount Assiniboine—often referred to as the “Matterhorn of the Rockies.”

“I think it’s so unique up here, it’s quite unlike anywhere else in the park that we have,” says Kaylee Richards, interpretive program assistant supervisor. “People can get a great birds-eye view.”

Hiking Trails & Activities

Beyond the viewing deck, Sunshine Meadows offers five family-friendly hiking trails that are consistently maintained and monitored. Visitors can explore independently or join a Trail Host for a one- or two-hour guided hike.

“The role of a guided walk would really be to explore the history of Sunshine, the geological events that happened here, how glaciers have helped shape the valley’s flora and fauna, and the skiing history of Sunshine,” says Collison.

Visitors looking for an intermediate hike can venture along Rock Isle Road, a 3.3-kilometre round-trip hike with views of Rock Isle Lake.

For a more challenging adventure, the Grizzly-Laryx Loop is one of Sunshine Meadows’ most rewarding hikes. The 2.5- to 3.5-hour round trip takes hikers past all three alpine lakes: Rock Isle, Laryx, and Grizzly Lake.

“It’s a pretty special moment when we speak to people in the summer and they’re like, ‘Wow, I had no idea this was out here,’” says Richards.

Those seeking views of the Monarch Ramparts can explore the Monarch Lookout Trail, while visitors looking for something beyond hiking can enjoy yoga in the Rockies, watercolour painting classes, live music at Trapper’s and an Indigenous Day celebration each August.

With so much to do, guests not ready to leave the mountain landscape can experience it into the evening with an overnight stay at Sunshine Mountain Lodge.

Sunshine Mountain Lodge

Sunshine Mountain Lodge offers a retreat after a day exploring the trails, allowing guests to relax and reconnect with the mountain landscape.

The lodge features one of Canada’s largest outdoor hot tubs, rejuvenating spa treatments, and a cedar-lined co-ed dry sauna. Additional amenities include a fitness room and activity space with a pool table, Wii, and flat-screen TV.

When it’s time to grub, Sunshine Mountain Lodge delivers some of the best dining in the Rockies, including two restaurants: Chimney Corner and Eagles Nest. Featuring sweeping mountain views through large bay windows and the comfort of two wood-burning fireplaces, Chimney Corner is open daily for breakfast and dinner and features outdoor terrace seating on sunny days.

Eagles Nest offers elevated fine-dining Canadian cuisine, while Java Lift Coffee serves locally roasted beverages, sandwiches, and freshly baked pastries.

All said, the boutique 84-room hotel provides a memorable mountain retreat for any occasion, whether it’s a girls’ getaway, romantic weekend, family trip, or solo escape. 

Conservation and Preservation

For those who work in Sunshine Meadows, protecting the landscape is as important as sharing the experience.  

“The biggest part for me, and what I see daily, is how important this ecosystem is. Not just for bears, but for all the wildlife that cross through here,” Collison said.

Collison says protecting Sunshine Meadows requires visitors to understand that even small actions can have an impact.

“Even if we were the best hiker in the world and we left no trace, there’s still a trace,” Collison said.

Sunshine Meadows is part of a larger alpine ecosystem supporting more than 20 species at risk throughout Banff National Park, including whitebark pine, little brown myotis bats, black swifts, wolverines and grizzly bears. Preserving this fragile ecosystem is a responsibility shared by everyone who visits.

That message is at the heart of the Sunshine Meadows Interpretive Centre, where guests learn about the areas natural and cultural history before heading onto the trails.

“It offers guests a brief history of the area, how Sunshine came to be, information about the wildlife and our flower boards that show what’s currently in bloom,” said Richards.

“Part of our role is giving an orientation talk to every guest who comes up to Sunshine,” Richards said. “Our purpose is to educate guests about the area they’re entering and to share the message about preserving and protecting the environment.”

Beyond educating visitors, Richards said the summer crew also works with Parks Canada and B.C. Parks on trail audits and other studies to monitor the health of the environment.

Richards hopes visitors leave Sunshine Meadows with more than photographs.

“We’re really high on that education piece, because it is such a unique environment that we have and I think we all feel very strongly to protect it,” Richards said. “I hope people appreciate the beauty of this place and take the values that we hold dear, to protect the environment, to wherever they go next.”

Every summer, as snow retreats and wildflowers return, Sunshine Meadows reveals a side of Banff National Park few places can match. It’s truly an island in the sky where panoramic ridges, rich biodiversity and a commitment to conservation come together, leaving visitors with a deeper connection to the park and a greater appreciation for one of Canada’s most extraordinary mountain landscapes.
